descripcion_es: Common everyday phrasal verbs, their meaning and where the object goes.
resumen: A phrasal verb is a verb followed by a particle (up, off, out, on…) that together have their own meaning. You have to learn them as vocabulary and check whether they can be separated.

filas: start / stop a machine or light (es: encender / apagar)
She looks after her little brother.
stop (a habit), stop trying (es: dejar, rendirse)
He gave up smoking last year.
I found out the truth yesterday.
I'll pick you up at the station.
have a good relationship with (es: llevarse bien con)
I get on well with my colleagues.

explicacion.texto: Separable: the object can go between the verb and the particle or after it: Turn the TV off / Turn off the TV. But if the object is a pronoun, it ALWAYS goes in the middle: Turn it off (not Turn off it).

Inseparable: the object always goes after the particle, even if it is a pronoun: look for it, look after them, get on with her. If the verb has two particles (run out of, get on with), it is never separated.

items: Some take no object: get up, carry on, break down (stop working), grow up (become an adult).
The same phrasal verb can have several meanings: take off = remove (clothes) / leave the ground (a plane).
In formal register they often have a Latin-based equivalent: find out = discover; give up = abandon.

ejemplos.frase: Could you turn the music down? I'm trying to sleep.
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Puedes bajar la música? Estoy intentando dormir.

ejemplos.frase: Who looks after your dog when you travel?
ejemplos.traduccion: ¿Quién cuida de tu perro cuando viajas?

ejemplos.frase: Our car broke down on the motorway.
ejemplos.traduccion: Se nos averió el coche en la autopista.

ejemplos.frase: I grew up in a small town near Zaragoza.
ejemplos.traduccion: Me crié en un pueblo cerca de Zaragoza.

ejemplos.frase: The plane took off two hours late.
ejemplos.traduccion: El avión despegó con dos horas de retraso.

ejemplos.frase: Don't give up! You're almost there.
ejemplos.traduccion: ¡No te rindas! Ya casi lo tienes.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Put on it, it's cold outside.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: Put it on, it's cold outside.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: With a separable phrasal verb, the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.
Spanish “buscar” is look for; look alone means “mirar” (direct your eyes).

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: We have finished the coffee, there isn't more.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: We have run out of coffee.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Spanish “quedarse sin” is run out of.

ejercicios.frase: It's dark in here. Can you turn ___ the light?
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table of phrasal verbs in this unit: turn on means “make a light or machine work” and turn off “make it stop”. The clue is It's dark in here: if it is dark, you ask someone to switch the light on. It is a separable phrasal verb, so you could also say turn the light on.
ejercicios.traduccion: Aquí está oscuro. ¿Puedes encender la luz?

errores_previstos.explicacion: Turn off means “switch off”, the opposite of what the context requires (it is dark).
Turn in means “hand in” or, informally, “go to bed”; to switch something on, use turn on.

ejercicios.frase: My grandmother looks ___ the children when we work late.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: look after means “take care of”. The clue is the grandmother and the children while the parents are at work: the meaning is to take care of them. Look after is inseparable, so the object (the children) always goes after the particle.
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi abuela cuida de los niños cuando trabajamos hasta tarde.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Look for means “try to find”; it would say that the grandmother is searching for the children.
Look at means “direct your eyes at”; it does not mean take care of.
A copy of Spanish “cuidar de”: in English the particle is after.

ejercicios.frase: He gave ___ chocolate for a month.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: give up means “stop a habit” or “stop trying”. The clue is chocolate for a month: going without something for a period of time. Give up is separable (give it up) and, if what you stop is an activity, it takes -ing (give up smoking).
ejercicios.traduccion: Dejó el chocolate durante un mes.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Give out means “distribute” or “stop working”; it does not mean stop a habit.
Give off means “produce” (a smell, heat); it has nothing to do with stopping a habit.

ejercicios.frase: Please fill ___ the application form in black ink.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: fill in means “complete a form”. The clue is the application form, a form you have to complete with information. Fill in is the British form; in American English people say fill out, which means the same, so both in and out are accepted. It is separable: fill it in, fill the form in.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Fill in = complete a form; in American English, fill out (both are accepted).
ejercicios.traduccion: Por favor, rellene el formulario de solicitud con tinta negra.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Fill up means “make a container or tank full” (fill up the tank), not complete a form.
Fill on does not exist as a phrasal verb.

ejercicios.frase: We've run out ___ bread. Can you buy some?
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: run out of means “have none left” (es: quedarse sin). The clue is Can you buy some?, which shows that there is no bread left. It is a two-particle phrasal verb and, as this unit points out, it is never separated; the second particle, of, introduces what has been used up.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Run out of = have none left (es: quedarse sin).
ejercicios.traduccion: Se nos ha acabado el pan. ¿Puedes comprar?

errores_previstos.explicacion: A copy of Spanish “quedarse sin” or “salir de”: the particle after run out is of.
Run off means “leave quickly, run away”; it does not mean have none left.

ejercicios.frase: I need to ___ what time the exam starts.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: find out means “discover, learn”. The clue is what time the exam starts, a piece of information you need to get. It is the informal equivalent of discover, which this unit gives as the formal alternative.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tengo que averiguar a qué hora empieza el examen.

por_opcion.find out: Correct: discover a piece of information.
por_opcion.look after: Incorrect: it means “take care of”; it is used with people, animals or things that need attention (look after the children).
por_opcion.give up: Incorrect: it means “stop a habit” or “stop trying” (give up smoking).

ejercicios.frase: The meeting was going well, so we ___ until seven.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: carry on means “continue”. The clue is was going well and until seven: the meeting continued. Carry on takes no object in this sentence, as Rules and key points explains.
ejercicios.traduccion: La reunión iba bien, así que seguimos hasta las siete.

por_opcion.took off: Incorrect: it means “leave the ground” (a plane) or “remove” clothes; it makes no sense with a meeting.
por_opcion.got up: Incorrect: it means “get out of bed”; it does not mean continue.

ejercicios.frase: My new shoes hurt, so I ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: if the object is a pronoun, it always goes between the verb and the particle. The clue is them, which replaces my new shoes. Take off (remove clothes) is separable, so took them off.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Pronoun in the middle of a separable phrasal verb: took them off.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los zapatos nuevos me hacían daño, así que me los quité.

por_opcion.took off them: Incorrect: with a separable phrasal verb the pronoun cannot go after the particle.
por_opcion.took them off: Correct: the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle, with the right phrasal verb for removing clothes.
por_opcion.took them out: Incorrect: take out means “remove from inside” (from a box, a pocket); for clothes or shoes you are wearing, use take off.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table in this unit: get on with means “have a good relationship with”. The clue is your sister and the question about the relationship. It is a two-particle phrasal verb and it is not separated. Well is often added: get on well with.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Get on with = have a good relationship with.

por_opcion.get on with: Correct: have a good relationship with someone.
por_opcion.get up with: Incorrect: get up means “get out of bed” and is not combined with with in this sense.
por_opcion.get off: Incorrect: it means “leave” a bus, train, etc.; it does not express a personal relationship.

ejercicios.frase: I'll pick up you at eight.
respuestas: I'll pick you up at eight.
I will pick you up at eight.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: with a pronoun, the object always goes in the middle. The clue is you, the object pronoun of pick up (collect someone). The correct form is pick you up. The full form will is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With a pronoun: pick + you + up.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll pick up you at eight.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence uncorrected: the pronoun goes between pick and up.
The particle up is missing; pick alone means “choose” or “take” (flowers, fruit).

errores_previstos.respuesta: I'll you pick up at eight.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The object pronoun does not go before the verb as in Spanish (“te recogeré”).

ejercicios.frase: She is looking her passport everywhere.
respuestas: She is looking for her passport everywhere.
She's looking for her passport everywhere.
ejercicios.explicacion: This is the second typical mistake in this unit: Spanish “buscar” is look for; look alone means “direct your eyes”. The clue is her passport everywhere, which shows a search. For must be added after looking. The contraction she's is also accepted.
ejercicios.traduccion: Está buscando su pasaporte por todas partes.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She is looking her passport everywhere.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence uncorrected: for is missing.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She is looking at her passport everywhere.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Look at means “direct your eyes at”; it does not mean try to find.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She is searching her passport everywhere.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Search without for means “examine” the passport; trying to find it would be search for.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: if the object is a pronoun, it always goes between the verb and the particle. The clue is that the instructions ask you to replace the radio with a pronoun. The radio is a singular thing, so it is it, placed between turn and off.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: With a pronoun, the object goes between the verb and the particle.

errores_previstos.explicacion: With a pronoun, turn off must be separated: Turn it off.
For a thing, use it; her is for female people.
Without off it means “rotate it”; the particle is essential.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule for separable verbs: when the object is a noun, it can go between the verb and the particle or after it. The clue is your coat, a noun, and put on (start wearing clothes), which is separable. That is why both put your coat on and put on your coat are correct.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Put on is separable: the noun can go in the middle or after.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle cannot go before the verb.
The particle cannot separate the possessive from its noun: your coat stays together.

ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the rule from Rules and key points: some phrasal verbs take no object, such as grow up (become an adult, be brought up). The clue is the question with where and did: the particle up stays at the end because there is no object after it. The order is where + did + subject + grow up.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Grow up takes no object; the particle stays at the end.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The particle goes after the verb: grow up.
In a direct question, did goes before the subject.

descripcion_larga_es: Phrasal verbs are verbs followed by a particle (up, off, out, on…) that together have their own meaning, often impossible to guess: give up means “stop a habit” and find out means “discover”. They are everywhere in spoken English and you have to learn them as vocabulary. Spanish speakers find them hard because Spanish does not have this construction and because you need to know whether they can be separated and where the pronoun goes.

contexto.que_es: A phrasal verb is the combination of a verb and one or two particles (adverbs or prepositions) that form a single unit of meaning. Some are separable (the object can go between the verb and the particle), others are inseparable, and some take no object.
contexto.por_que_importa: In conversation and informal texts, phrasal verbs replace many Latin-based verbs (find out for discover, give up for abandon), so without them you understand little real English and speak in a stiff way. Putting the pronoun in the wrong place (turn off it) or changing the particle alters the meaning or sounds clearly foreign.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In everyday life: routines (get up), clothes (put on, take off), devices (turn on, turn off), paperwork (fill in), relationships (get on with). Formal register usually prefers the equivalent Latin-based verb. Spanish speakers tend to leave out the particle (look my keys for look for my keys) or to put the pronoun at the end as in Spanish.
